name: Hawthorn (Crataegus)
short: One heart-failure trial had more adverse events (a larger one did not) and, in retrospective analysis, more early worsening. Digoxin: lab study says avoid; no significant level change in 8 volunteers.
text: A systematic review of safety data on hawthorn single-herb preparations covered 24 clinical studies with data from 5,577 patients and counted 166 adverse events, most of them mild to moderate; the most frequent were gastrointestinal complaints, dizziness or vertigo, palpitation, headache and migraine. Eight severe adverse events were reported with one extract, and events in the trials included gastrointestinal haemorrhage (2) and circulation failure (2); the abstract does not say whether these were attributed to hawthorn. The reviewers concluded that hawthorn seems to be well tolerated even if some severe adverse events were reported, found no reports of drug interactions, and cautioned that unsupervised use can be associated with problems, especially with other medications. In heart failure, a 6-month placebo-controlled trial in 120 patients on standard therapy reported significantly more adverse events in the hawthorn group, most of them non-cardiac; a retrospective analysis of the same trial found no overall difference in heart failure progression (46.6% with hawthorn, 43.3% with placebo) but concluded that the extract appeared to increase the early risk of progression, and reported a significantly greater risk in patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less. In contrast, a 24-month placebo-controlled trial in 2681 patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction reported adverse events as comparable in both groups, with no significant effect on the time to a first cardiac event. For digoxin, a crossover study in 8 healthy volunteers found that 3 weeks of hawthorn did not significantly alter digoxin pharmacokinetics; a laboratory study found that hawthorn extract interfered with one of two digoxin blood-level immunoassays and, in isolated rat heart cells, acted in a way the authors interpreted as a pharmacodynamic interaction, and those authors advised that a patient receiving digoxin should avoid hawthorn.
